title: Cloze Test
summary: One short passage with five numbered blanks, attempted as a single set — 5 marks that reward method over memory. Most blanks are decided by the passage's tense anchor, clause logic or a fixed collocation, so a trained routine converts cloze into the most reliable scoring block in the English section.

subtopics.title: What a cloze test is and how to attack it
subtopics.concept:
A cloze test is one short passage — usually 100–150 words — in which 5 words have been removed and numbered. Each question asks you to restore one blank. The passage is a *network*: every sentence you read constrains what the blanks can be, which is why cloze rewards a fixed method far more than raw vocabulary.

**The 5-step SSC method:**
1. Read the whole passage once, ignoring the blanks as far as possible. Fix the theme and the time frame (past narrative? general present? future plan?).
2. Note the tense anchor: the opening sentences usually fix the tense that most verb blanks must follow.
3. For each blank, *predict your own word* from the sentence's meaning before looking at the options.
4. Match options against your prediction; when none match, fall back to elimination by grammar (number, tense, part of speech) and logic.
5. After marking all five, read the completed passage once — it must sound like ordinary prose. Any jarring blank is usually a wrong choice.

| Blank type | What decides the answer | First check |
|---|---|---|
| Verb form / tense | time anchors in surrounding sentences + subject number | find the anchor word (yesterday, every day, since, by evening) |
| Connector | the logical relation between the two clauses it joins | ask: contrast, cause, result or addition? |
| Preposition / phrasal verb | fixed collocation of the neighbouring word | identify the governing verb/adjective/noun |
| Noun / vocabulary | meaning that fits the sentence AND the passage theme | predict your own word before reading options |
| Article / determiner | sound of the next word + which-inference (specific or not) | say the phrase aloud |

**Time budget:** under two minutes for the full read, 20–30 seconds per blank, 30 seconds for the final read-through. Attempt cloze in one sitting — the passage lives in your short-term memory only while the set is open.

**Never solve blanks in isolation.** An option that fits its own sentence but contradicts the passage's tense or theme is a planted trap; the final read-through exists to catch exactly this.

tricks.title: Tense anchor first
tricks.body: Before touching any blank, underline the time expressions: 'Every morning...', 'Last month...', 'by evening'. Verb blanks and even prepositions obey these anchors.

example.q: Passage opens 'Every morning, before the city fully ___' — options: awaken / awakens / awakened / is awaken.
example.solution: Anchor 'every morning' = habitual present; subject 'city' = singular → awakens.

tricks.title: Predict, then match
tricks.body: Cover the options with your hand, read the sentence, and whisper your own word. Options are written to include your word's exact meaning — anything far from it is usually wrong.

tricks.title: The read-aloud finish
tricks.body: After answering all five, read the passage silently as if it were written by someone else. Grammar errors and logic breaks become audible — re-check any blank where you stumble.

mistakes: Answering blank by blank without reading the full passage first — you lose every cross-blank clue.
Changing tense midway: a past-tense narrative forces past forms on later verb blanks.
Choosing a word that fits the sentence's topic but not its logic (e.g. a cause-word where a contrast is needed).
Spending equal time on every blank; easy grammar blanks take 15 seconds, bank that time for the vocabulary blank.
subtopics.notes:
### What is a cloze test?
A cloze test is a short passage — usually 80 to 150 words — in which several words are removed and numbered (1), (2), (3)… For every blank you get four options, and you pick the word that best fits **both the grammar and the meaning** of that place. SSC, Railway and Banking papers commonly ask 5 blanks from one passage, each blank as a separate question that shares the same story.

A cloze passage is like a wall with a few bricks missing. You cannot choose a brick by looking at the hole alone — you must look at the wall around it.

### The five-step routine
1. **Read the whole passage once**, ignoring the options. Fix the theme (a village lake, a new rule, an old memory) and the time frame (past story, present habit, future plan).
2. **Read the sentence with the blank twice** — the part before the blank and the part after it. The clue usually sits on one of these two sides.
3. **Try every option inside the full sentence**, never as a word alone. A word may look right on its own and break the sentence.
4. **Reject in two rounds.** First cut options that break a rule (wrong verb form, wrong agreement). Then cut options that are grammatical but do not fit the meaning.
5. **Re-read the finished passage** with your answers filled in. The whole thing must sound like natural English from the first line to the last.

### The four kinds of blanks
| Blank type | What decides the answer |
|---|---|
| Grammar (verb form, agreement, article, pronoun) | A rule: subject number, time frame, linking verb |
| Vocabulary (noun, verb, adjective choice) | Meaning and collocation |
| Connector (but, because, moreover) | The direction between two clauses |
| Preposition / phrasal verb | A fixed usage or the particle's meaning |

Most papers mix all four kinds in one passage, so one passage tests four small skills.

### Order of solving
Answer the easiest blank first, even if it is blank (5). A solved blank often makes its neighbours easier, because one more slot of the story is filled. Leave a stubborn blank for the last round; with most of the passage filled, it usually resolves itself. Mark skipped blanks on the question paper so you do not lose count.

### A worked blank
Blank: "The morning walk costs nothing and demands no equipment, (1) ______ very few people manage to continue it beyond a fortnight."
Options: because / yet / hence / so.
The first clause praises the walk (+), the second says few continue it (−). Opposite directions need a contrast word: **yet**. *So* and *hence* would wrongly make failure a result of the walk's simplicity, and *because* reverses the logic. This is the connector decision in action.

### Traps that cost marks
- **Right grammar, wrong meaning**: all four options may be verbs in the correct form; only one matches the sentence's sense.
- **Right meaning, wrong form**: the word you want appears in a wrong shape (*develop* instead of *develops*).
- **Local fit, passage clash**: an option may fit its own sentence and still contradict a line two sentences later — for example, a "problem" the passage has already solved.
- **Ignoring the time frame**: if the story is set in the past ("Last year…"), a present-tense option is wrong even if it sounds fine.

### Time plan
Five blanks should take four to five minutes. Never spend more than a minute on one blank in the first round.

### Quick revision
- Read the full passage before touching the options.
- Try each option inside the full sentence.
- Grammar blanks → rule; vocab blanks → meaning; connectors → clause direction; prepositions → fixed usage.
- Solve easy blanks first, re-read at the end.
- Two rounds of elimination: form first, then meaning.

patterns.name: Blank whose answer needs the passage's overall theme
patterns.howToSpot: Several options are grammatical and each could fit some sentence; only one continues the passage's controlling idea or metaphor.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the whole passage and name its theme in five words.
2. Ask which option keeps that theme running in this sentence.
3. Cut options that are real words but belong to a different world (an office word in a farming story).

*Why it works:* a cloze passage is one connected story; the writer keeps one metaphor or topic alive, and the blank is part of it.

example.q: Passage about a night market: "The market sells food, but what it really (1) ______ is company." (a) paints (b) sells (c) measures (d) imports
example.solution: The passage's metaphor is selling. "Sells company" continues it. Answer: **(b) sells**.

patterns.name: All four options grammatical — meaning decides
patterns.howToSpot: Every option is the same part of speech in the correct form, so no rule can cut them.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the sentence and say its meaning in your own words.
2. Put each option in the blank and read the full sentence.
3. Keep the one that says what the sentence actually says; cut options that are merely about the same topic.

*Why it works:* when grammar is equal, the setter is testing careful reading, not vocabulary size.

example.q: "Students check the taps after (1) ______ and repair dripping ones the same day." (a) applause (b) assembly (c) gravity (d) thunder
example.solution: Only *assembly* is a school event that happens before students could check taps. Answer: **(b) assembly**.

patterns.name: The clue sits in a neighbouring sentence
patterns.howToSpot: The blank's own sentence feels incomplete; the word that fits is confirmed one sentence earlier or later.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the sentence before AND after the blank.
2. Look for a repeated idea or word pair (tankers, then a single tanker again).
3. Choose the option that completes that cross-sentence link.

*Why it works:* cloze passages are short, so writers deliberately repeat or answer ideas one line apart.

example.q: "The school used to buy tankers of water every summer. … This summer it did not order a single (1) ______." (a) ticket (b) book (c) tanker (d) rule
example.solution: Sentence 1 sets the pair *buy tankers → order a single tanker*. Answer: **(c) tanker**.

patterns.name: Option fits the sentence but clashes with the passage
patterns.howToSpot: Two options seem to fit the blank; re-reading another line shows one of them contradicts the story.
patterns.logic:
1. Do not answer on the first plausible option.
2. Re-read the full passage with each survivor filled in.
3. Drop the option that clashes with a later or earlier line.

*Why it works:* the setter places a 'local' option that ignores the whole story; the final re-read catches it.

example.q: "The tank taught them what the (1) ______ never did — that water is counted." The passage is about school students. (a) plumber (b) syllabus (c) generator (d) noticeboard
example.solution: Only a syllabus is something that *teaches* in a school. Re-reading shows the lesson is academic, not a plumbing job. Answer: **(b) syllabus**.

subtopics.title: Grammar inside the passage: tense, agreement, articles
subtopics.concept:
Most cloze blanks are won by grammar before vocabulary. Three systems matter.

**Tense.** The passage's opening fixes its time frame. A habitual opening ('Every morning...') demands simple present for habitual verbs; a past narrative ('When Arun was small...') demands past forms for events inside the story; 'still ___' with a present meaning demands present perfect or simple present, never past. Watch result words like *by evening / by the time*, which often need perfect forms — but only when the sentence truly looks back from a later point, not in simple narrative sequence.

**Subject–verb agreement.** SSC hides the subject between the blank and its neighbours: 'a group that walks together ___ its own discipline' — the subject is *a group* (singular), not *walks* or *discipline*. Strip the phrase to 'a group ___' and choose. Plurals to watch: *each, every, either, neither, everyone* → singular; *a number of* → plural, *the number of* → singular.

**Articles and determiners.** *A/an* is decided by sound, not spelling: *a university, an hour, a European, an MLA*. *The* appears when the noun is already known, unique, or specified by the phrase after it.

**Two-step verification for verb blanks:** (1) Does the tense match the passage anchor? (2) Does the form match the subject? An option passing only one test is a designed distractor.

tricks.title: Strip-to-subject
tricks.body: Delete every phrase between the subject and the verb blank, then apply agreement to the bare skeleton.

example.q: 'A group that walks together ___ its own quiet discipline.' Options: develop / develops / developing / developed(no context).
example.solution: Skeleton: 'a group ___ discipline' → singular + habitual present → develops.

tricks.title: Only-one-past trick
tricks.body: When a narrative blank offers just one past-tense option among present/gerund forms, the anchor already decided it — mark it and move on without re-reading the paragraph.

tricks.title: Say the article aloud
tricks.body: For a/an blanks, pronounce the *next word's first sound*: 'an hour' but 'a university'. Silent letters and 'yu' sounds decide it, not the first letter.

mistakes: Agreeing the verb with the nearest noun instead of the true subject.
Using a perfect tense ('had joined') where plain narrative past is required, because 'by evening' looks like a perfect anchor.
Choosing the base verb form after a singular subject ('the city awaken').
Picking 'an' before words beginning with a vowel letter that is pronounced as a consonant ('a one-rupee coin').
subtopics.notes:
### Grammar blanks: what is really tested
In most cloze passages, three or four of the five blanks are decided by a grammar rule, not by word power. The passage fixes a setting — time, subject, structure — and the blank must obey it. Learn the six checks below and most grammar blanks answer themselves.

### 1. Subject-verb agreement
Find the true subject — the noun the verb belongs to — and ignore the words packed between it and the verb.
- Correct: The quality of the mangoes **is** poor. Incorrect: The quality of the mangoes **are** poor. (subject = quality)
- Correct: Every one of the players **was** tired. Incorrect: Every one of the players **were** tired. (*each, every, either, neither, one of + plural noun* take a singular verb)
- Correct: The list of items **is** on the table. Incorrect: The list of items **are** on the table.

### 2. The time frame (tense)
The first sentence usually sets the tense for the whole passage, and every verb must stay inside that frame.
- "When Arun was small…" → past narrative → Correct: he **drafted** a reply. Incorrect: he **drafts** a reply.
- Habits and general truths → simple present: Correct: The shop **opens** at nine. Incorrect: The shop **opened** at nine (in a habitual passage).
- Signal words: *yesterday, last year, ago* → past; *now, still, these days, every morning* → present; *since, for, already, yet* → perfect forms.
- But a habit inside a past story can stay past: "Every evening he **made** new kites" (past habit of that story).

### 3. Verb forms: finite, gerund, infinitive
Only a finite verb can act as the main verb. After certain words, a non-finite form is compulsory:
- *enjoy, avoid, mind, finish, suggest, keep* + **-ing**: Correct: He enjoys **showing** old kites. Incorrect: He enjoys **to show** old kites.
- *decide, plan, hope, refuse, manage, teach someone* + **to + base form**: Correct: Gardening has taught him **to be** patient. Incorrect: Gardening has taught him **being** patient.
- *preposition + -ing*: Correct: She is good **at solving** puzzles. Incorrect: She is good **at to solve** puzzles.
- A bare -ing form cannot serve as the finite verb: Incorrect: A group **developing** its own discipline. Correct: A group **develops** its own discipline.

### 4. Articles: a, an, the
- **a/an** = first mention or one of many: He gave him **a** bucket the very next day.
- **the** = already known, or one of a kind: **The** sky above the lane was full of kites.
- No article for most plural or general nouns: Correct: **Trees give shade.** Incorrect: **The trees give shade** (when trees in general are meant).
- a + consonant sound, an + vowel sound: **a university** (yoo-sound), **an hour** (silent h).

### 5. Adjective or adverb?
After a linking verb (*be, look, seem, feel, taste, smell, sound*) use an adjective:
- Correct: The tree looks **attractive**. Incorrect: The tree looks **attractively**.
- After an action verb use an adverb: Correct: She sings **beautifully**.

### 6. Pronouns
A pronoun must match its noun in number and gender, and its case must fit the job — subject (*I, he, they*), object (*me, him, them*), possessive (*my, his, their*).
- Correct: The committee published **its** report. Incorrect: The committee published **their's** report.
- Correct: Between you and **me**, the plan is weak. Incorrect: Between you and **I**, the plan is weak.

### Quick revision
- Find the true subject first; ignore the words between it and the verb.
- Fix the passage's time frame, then keep every verb inside it.
- enjoy/avoid + -ing; decide/refuse/teach + to; preposition + -ing.
- a/an = first mention; the = known or one-of-a-kind.
- Linking verb + adjective; action verb + adverb.
- Pronoun = same number and gender as its noun, right case for the job.

patterns.name: Subject-verb agreement blank
patterns.howToSpot: The options are forms of the same verb (give/gives/gave) and the sentence has a long subject phrase or an each/every/one-of structure.
patterns.logic:
1. Cross out the phrase between the subject and the verb.
2. Ask: is the true subject singular or plural?
3. Match the verb, then check the passage's time frame (present or past).

*Why it works:* the setter hides the subject behind a prepositional phrase so that the nearest noun misleads you.

example.q: "The soil in his yard (1) ______ too rocky for beds." (a) is (b) are (c) were (d) be
example.solution: True subject = soil (singular), passage is in present → **is**. *Are* is pulled by the nearby plural feel; *were* breaks the present frame.

patterns.name: Tense / time-frame blank
patterns.howToSpot: The options are the same verb in different tenses and the passage has a clear anchor: 'Last January', 'now', 'every morning'.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the time anchor of the sentence or passage.
2. Past anchor → simple past; habit in the story → past habitual; present anchor (now, still) → simple present.
3. Never let one verb drift out of the passage's frame.

*Why it works:* narratives hold one tense; a wrong-tense option sounds fine alone but breaks the story.

example.q: "Last January the terrace became a workshop. Every evening he and his son (1) ______ new kites." (a) made (b) make (c) making (d) maker
example.solution: Anchor 'Last January' → past narrative, habitual 'every evening' → simple past: **made**. *Make* breaks the frame; *making* is not finite.

patterns.name: Verb form: gerund or infinitive after another word
patterns.howToSpot: The blank follows a verb like enjoy/avoid or decide/teach, or follows a preposition.
patterns.logic:
1. Identify the word before the blank.
2. enjoy, avoid, mind, finish, suggest → -ing form.
3. decide, hope, refuse, manage, teach someone → to + base form.
4. After a preposition → -ing form.

*Why it works:* these verbs and prepositions fix the form of the next verb; no meaning decision is needed.

example.q: "He enjoys (1) ______ old kites to the children of the lane." (a) showing (b) show (c) to show (d) showed
example.solution: *Enjoy* takes the -ing form: **showing**. 'Enjoys to show' is wrong in English.

patterns.name: Article / determiner blank
patterns.howToSpot: The options are a, an, the (or their capital forms) before a noun.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask if the noun is already known or one of a kind → the.
2. First mention, one of many → a/an (an before a vowel SOUND).
3. General plural or uncountable idea → no article, so pick the option that works as a zero article if offered.

*Why it works:* article choice follows three simple conditions; the sentence usually makes one condition obvious.

example.q: "On festival day (1) ______ sky above the lane was so full of kites that the birds kept their distance." (a) A (b) An (c) The (d) Some
example.solution: There is one sky above the lane and the phrase adds 'above the lane' (already specific): **The**. 'A sky' would mean one of several skies.

subtopics.title: Vocabulary blanks: meaning, register and collocation
subtopics.concept:
Vocabulary blanks ask which *word* completes the sentence. Two filters decide, in order:

**1. Meaning filter.** The word must make the sentence true to the passage's logic. Read the sentence, note what idea is missing ('benefits depend on ___; twenty minutes on Sunday cannot undo six days of sitting' → the missing idea is *consistency*), then find the option naming that idea (*regularity*).

**2. Register filter.** SSC passages are written in neutral, slightly formal prose. Between two words of equal meaning, the neutral-formal one wins: *children* beats *kids*, *assistance* beats *a helping hand*, *begin* beats *kick off*. Slangy, poetic or babyish options are decoration.

**Collocation filter (often decisive).** Some words are only valid beside their partners: *gain momentum* (not *obtain momentum*), *pay attention* (not *give attention*), *heavy rain* (not *strong rain*), *do homework* (not *make homework*). When two options both fit the meaning, the collocation decides.

**Positive/negative fit.** Check the sentence's emotional direction. 'does more than look ___' in a passage praising trees wants a positive word (*attractive*); a criticism wants a negative one. An option of the wrong polarity is wrong regardless of meaning.

tricks.title: Name the missing idea
tricks.body: Before looking down, say what the sentence lacks in plain words: 'it needs the idea of CONSISTENCY here'. Then choose the option that says it — this defeats look-alike distractors.

example.q: '...its benefits depend almost entirely on ___; twenty minutes on Sunday cannot undo six days of sitting.'
example.solution: Missing idea = doing it regularly → regularity (not equipment, luck or medicine).

tricks.title: Collocation pairs to bank
tricks.body: Memorise high-frequency pairs: gain momentum, pay attention, take measures, reach a decision, bear fruit, meet a deadline, break the news, strike a balance. Cloze nouns and verbs revolve around them.

tricks.title: Polarity check
tricks.body: Mark the sentence + or − before choosing. A praising sentence rejects negative words even when they are grammatically perfect.

mistakes: Choosing a word that fits the passage's *topic* instead of the sentence's *meaning*.
Overlooking fixed pairs and choosing a near-synonym that no native writer would put in that slot.
Selecting a big dictionary word when the passage's simple register wants the simple word.
Forgetting that the same blank may be constrained by the NEXT sentence, not just its own.
subtopics.notes:
### Vocabulary blanks: meaning in context
A vocabulary blank gives four options that are all grammatically correct. No rule can save you here — only the sentence's meaning can. The skill is reading the sentence closely enough that the missing word almost appears by itself.

### Where the clue sits
Usually in the same sentence; sometimes in the next one.
- Same sentence: "Benefits depend almost entirely on (1) ______; twenty minutes on Sunday cannot undo six days of sitting." The clause after the semicolon *defines* the answer — the idea of doing something again and again → **regularity**.
- Next sentence: "The traders did not take the plan lying down. They collected signatures…" The second sentence tells you the first blank needs a resistance word.

### Collocations decide many blanks
Some words travel together so firmly that the pair is one unit:
- **take** advantage, **take** pride, **take** a decision
- **make** room, **make** a mistake, **make** progress
- **pay** attention, **pay** a fine, **pay** a visit
- **keep** a promise, **keep** records, **break** a rule
If the blank is half of such a pair, the collocation decides, and the other three options die at once — however sensible they sound alone. Correct: She **took** full advantage of the offer. Incorrect: She **did** full advantage of the offer.

### The tone test
Decide whether the sentence praises or blames, hopes or fears. The word must carry the same feeling.
- "Doctors praised the ___ results" → positive: **remarkable**, not *dreadful*.
- "Officials are tempted to ___ corners" → negative: **cut**, not *decorate*.
A grammatically perfect option with the wrong tone is a classic trap.

### Near-synonyms are not equal
Options are often close: *quality / standard / character / grade*, or *preserve / protect / defend*. Compare them against the exact noun in the sentence: "the quiet here has a different ___" → quiet has a **quality**, not a standard or grade. When two options both fit, check which one the passage's level of language matches — a plain narrative does not suddenly use an official word.

### The elimination method for vocab blanks
1. Mark each option + (fits), − (wrong meaning), ? (possible).
2. Keep the + options; a ? option must be justified by a clear clue, not by hope.
3. If two survive, plug both into the WHOLE passage — the passage usually rejects one.

### Worked example
Blank: "Pleased by the response, the corporation has sanctioned two more fans, and the students (1) ______ full advantage of the extended hours." Options: make / do / take / give.
The collocation is **take advantage of**. Answer: take. *Do* and *make* are the classic Indian-English trap for this pair.

### Quick revision
- Vocab blanks are decided by meaning, collocation and tone — not by grammar.
- The clue is usually in the same sentence; read the next one too.
- Learn pairs: take advantage, make room, pay attention, keep a promise.
- Match the sentence's feeling: praise word in a praising line.
- Near-synonyms: test each against the exact noun in the sentence.
- Two survivors → plug both into the whole passage.

patterns.name: Noun choice by context
patterns.howToSpot: All four options are singular/plural nouns that fit the grammar; the sentence's meaning and the surrounding idea pick one.
patterns.logic:
1. Say the sentence's message in your own words.
2. Ask which noun names that message exactly.
3. Cut nouns that belong to the topic but not to this sentence.

*Why it works:* the setter chooses three nouns from the same broad field; only one matches the precise idea.

example.q: "Regulars say the quiet here has a different (1) ______ from the quiet of their homes." (a) price (b) quality (c) length (d) colour
example.solution: The passage contrasts two kinds of quiet — their character differs. Quiet has a **quality**, not a price or length. Answer: **(b) quality**.

patterns.name: Verb choice by context
patterns.howToSpot: Four verbs, all grammatical after the subject; meaning and the object of the verb decide.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the verb's object and the sentence's logic.
2. Ask what action the story describes here.
3. Plug each verb in with its object and keep the one that makes a real action.

*Why it works:* wrong verbs are from the same field but name a different action (publish vs preserve).

example.q: "The librarian has also begun to (1) ______ old newspapers for a small archive." (a) publish (b) preserve (c) repair (d) translate
example.solution: The archive keeps old papers safe → **preserve**. Publishing makes new copies; repairing fixes damage; translating changes language — none is 'store for the future'.

patterns.name: Adjective choice by tone and contrast
patterns.howToSpot: Four adjectives fit before the noun; the sentence's feeling or a contrast word (once…now, but) picks one.
patterns.logic:
1. Look for a contrast signal (once, now, but, although).
2. Choose the adjective that sits on the other side of the contrast.
3. Check the tone: praise line → positive adjective.

*Why it works:* contrast sentences demand opposite poles; only one option stands opposite the stated pole.

example.q: "The reading hall, once half (1) ______, is now full by eight o'clock." (a) painted (b) carpeted (c) empty (d) furnished
example.solution: Contrast: once half ___ → now full. The opposite of full is **empty**. Painted/carpeted/furnished do not stand against 'full'.

patterns.name: Collocation blank (verb + fixed noun)
patterns.howToSpot: The blank completes a set phrase: take advantage, make room, pay attention, keep a promise.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the noun that follows the blank.
2. Recall the fixed partner verb for that noun.
3. Do not translate from your mother tongue — Indian English often swaps make/do/take.

*Why it works:* collocations are conventions, not logic; only the conventional partner is correct.

example.q: "The traders now (1) ______ room for her boards every Sunday morning." (a) do (b) take (c) make (d) give
example.solution: The fixed phrase is **make room for** = clear space for. 'Do room', 'take room' are not English; 'give room' would need 'to someone' in a different sense.

subtopics.title: Connector blanks: contrast, cause, result, addition
subtopics.concept:
A connector blank is a logic question in disguise. The option must name the exact relation between the clause before and the clause after.

**Two-clause test.** Split the sentence at the blank and ask how clause B behaves toward clause A:
- B pulls *against* A → contrast: **yet, but, however, although, still, whereas**.
- B explains *why* A is true → cause: **because, since, as**.
- B is the *outcome* of A → result: **so, therefore, hence, thus**.
- B *adds* a parallel point → addition: **moreover, besides, also, and**.

| Relation | Connectors | Mini-test |
|---|---|---|
| Contrast | but, yet, however, although, whereas, still | the two clauses pull in opposite directions |
| Cause | because, since, as, for | second clause explains why the first is true |
| Result | so, therefore, hence, thus, consequently | second clause is the outcome of the first |
| Addition | moreover, besides, also, and, furthermore | second clause adds a parallel point |
| Condition | if, unless, provided | one clause depends on the other happening |
| Time | when, while, before, after, until | one clause fixes when the other happens |

**Signature SSC item:** praise followed by limitation. 'The walk costs nothing and demands no equipment, ___ very few people continue it' — the second clause concedes a limit, so *yet/but* is required; *so* or *because* breaks the logic. Train your ear on this pattern: it appears in nearly every paper.

**Placement grammar.** *However* and *therefore* need a comma and usually start a new sentence or clause ('..., however,'), while *yet/but/so* join clauses directly after a comma. If the blank sits between two clauses joined by a comma, the joining connector is grammatically safer.

**Double-connector pairs:** *not only... but also*, *either... or*, *neither... nor*, *both... and*, *no sooner... than*, *hardly... when*, *lest... should*. If one half appears outside the blank, only its partner can fill the blank.

tricks.title: Opposite-direction test
tricks.body: Give each clause a + or − sign. Same signs → addition/result connector; opposite signs → contrast connector.

example.q: 'The walk costs nothing and demands no equipment (+), ___ very few people continue it (−).'
example.solution: + then − → contrast → yet/but. 'So' or 'because' would need matching directions.

tricks.title: Partner hunt
tricks.body: Scan the sentence for the other half of a correlative pair. Seeing 'not only' fixes the blank to 'but also' — zero thinking needed.

tricks.title: Comma tell
tricks.body: 'clause, ___ clause' with a single-word slot wants *yet/but/so/for/and*. Options like 'however/therefore' fit 'clause. ___, clause' patterns instead.

mistakes: Confusing result (*so*) with cause (*because*) — read which clause explains which.
Choosing 'although' where a plain 'but' is needed: *although* cannot join two independent clauses without restructuring.
Ignoring the passage's flow: a connector that fits the sentence but reverses the paragraph's argument is wrong.
Marking 'and' as always safe; in a concession context it destroys the author's point.
subtopics.notes:
### Connector blanks: one logic decision
A connector blank joins two clauses, and your only job is to find the **direction** between them: same way or opposite way, cause or result, one event after another. The connector is logic written as a single word.

### Step 1: find the two clauses
Read the words on both sides of the blank and compress each side into a sign:
- "The walk costs nothing **(+)**, ___ very few continue it **(−)**" → opposite directions → contrast.
- "It rained heavily **(+cause)**, ___ the match was cancelled **(−result)**" → cause and result.
- "Prices rose **(point 1)**, ___ wages stayed flat **(point 2)**" → the writer adds a second, parallel point.
- "She finished her homework **(event 1)**, ___ the lights went out **(event 2)**" → time order or overlap.

### Step 2: pick the family, then the word
| Family | Direction | Members often seen |
|---|---|---|
| Contrast | the two clauses pull apart | but, yet, however, whereas, although, while |
| Result | A happened, so B happened | so, therefore, hence, thus, as a result |
| Reason | B is why A happened | because, since, as, for |
| Addition | a second, supporting point | moreover, furthermore, besides, also, in addition |
| Time | events in order or overlap | when, while, before, after, until, as soon as |
| Condition | one depends on the other | if, unless, provided |

### Step 3: use the punctuation clue
- A semicolon or full stop, then a comma after the blank → a linking adverb: **however, moreover, therefore, otherwise**. ("Business has not suffered; **moreover**, some customers order a second cup.")
- A comma inside one sentence joining two clauses → **but, so, because, and**.
- Beginning of a second sentence → the connector often looks back at the whole first sentence.

### Common confusions
- **but vs so**: "The shop is small, ___ it is always full." → but (opposite). "The road was cleared, ___ traffic flowed again." → so (result).
- **because vs although**: "___ it rained, the match went on." → Although (surprising result). "___ it rained, the match was cancelled." → Because (normal result).
- **while**: two meanings — time overlap ("read **while** the tea cools") and contrast ("cities grew rich, **while** villages lagged").
- **until**: an action continues up to a time point: "He waited **until** morning."

### Method in the exam
1. Read both sides of the blank; write + or − over each.
2. Same direction → addition, result or time; opposite → contrast; effect needs a cause → reason.
3. Try the chosen word: the finished sentence must sound like something a newspaper would print.

### Quick revision
- Connector = the direction between two clauses; find the clauses first.
- Contrast: but, yet, however, although, whereas. Result: so, therefore, hence. Reason: because, since. Addition: moreover, besides. Time: when, while, until, before.
- Semicolon + comma → however/moreover/therefore/otherwise.
- because vs although: normal result vs surprising result.
- Test the word by reading the full joined sentence aloud.

patterns.name: Contrast connector (but, yet, although, whereas)
patterns.howToSpot: The clause before and after the blank point in opposite directions, or the second clause surprises you after the first.
patterns.logic:
1. Compress each clause to a sign: + or −, advantage or disadvantage.
2. Opposite signs → contrast family.
3. Choose the member that fits the punctuation: mid-sentence comma → but/yet/although; new sentence → however; two parallel facts → whereas.

*Why it works:* contrast is the commonest single logic in short passages; every other option breaks one side of the pair.

example.q: "His regulars first laughed at the shelf, (1) ______ today even senior nurses borrow his weeklies." (a) so (b) but (c) because (d) and
example.solution: Laughed (−) → borrow now (+): opposite directions → **but**. *So* would make laughing the cause of borrowing.

patterns.name: Reason connector (because, since, as)
patterns.howToSpot: One clause gives the cause and the other the effect; the blank sits before the cause part (or the question 'why?' fits between the clauses).
patterns.logic:
1. Ask which clause answers 'why' for the other.
2. If the blank introduces the why-clause → because/since/as.
3. Reject result words (so, therefore) — they would reverse the direction.

*Why it works:* learners confuse reason and result; the test is which clause could be the answer to 'why'.

example.q: "Nurses borrow the weeklies (1) ______ the magazines remind them of the hospital's own reading room." (a) unless (b) although (c) because (d) until
example.solution: The second clause explains the borrowing: **because**. *Although* needs a surprise, not a reason.

patterns.name: Addition connector (moreover, furthermore, besides)
patterns.howToSpot: The second sentence or clause adds another point of the same kind — usually after a semicolon, then a comma.
patterns.logic:
1. Check that both clauses push the same way (both benefits or both problems).
2. Semicolon + comma → linking adverb: moreover, furthermore, in addition.
3. Reject contrast and result words; the writer is agreeing with himself, not turning.

*Why it works:* passages list two or three supports for one claim; the addition connector is the join.

example.q: "Business has not suffered at all; (1) ______, some customers now order a second cup to finish an article." (a) however (b) therefore (c) moreover (d) otherwise
example.solution: Same direction (business fine, then even better) → **moreover**. *However* turns, *therefore* claims a result.

patterns.name: Time connector (while, until, before, after, when)
patterns.howToSpot: The two clauses describe events placed on a clock — overlapping, or one ending at a point.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask how the two events sit in time: together, one before the other, or up to a limit.
2. Overlapping actions → while/when; continues up to a point → until; earlier vs later → before/after.
3. Plug the word in and check the clock reading of the sentence.

*Why it works:* time words are precise; each option places the events differently, and only one matches the story.

example.q: "A scooter left at a public charging point after nine at night may stay there (1) ______ morning." (a) until (b) since (c) after (d) by
example.solution: The scooter waits from night up to a limit point: **until** morning. *Since* needs a starting point, *after* reverses the order.

subtopics.title: Preposition and phrasal-verb blanks
subtopics.concept:
Preposition blanks are pure collocation memory: the word before or after the blank dictates the answer.

**Find the governor.** The preposition belongs to a nearby verb, adjective or noun:
- depend **on**, insist **on**, congratulate **on**;
- afraid **of**, fond **of**, aware **of**;
- good **at**, angry **with** (person) / **at** (thing), married **to**;
- reason **for**, solution **to**, influence **on**, rise **in**.
Identify the governor, then recall its fixed partner — never translate meaning word by word.

**Phrasal-verb blanks** test verb + particle as one unit. The same verb changes meaning with each particle, so read the sentence's demand first, then match the unit: caring for trees → *look after*; investigating a complaint → *look into*; a road replacing a market → *give way to*.

| Phrasal verb | Meaning | Fit in a sentence |
|---|---|---|
| give way to | yield; be replaced by | the old market gave way to a mall |
| look after | take care of | residents look after the street trees |
| look into | investigate | the committee will look into the complaint |
| carry out | perform, execute | carry out a survey / an order |
| put off | postpone | the match was put off till Sunday |
| call off | cancel | the strike was called off |
| break out | begin suddenly (fire, war, disease) | a fire broke out at night |
| turn down | reject | she turned down the offer |
| come across | meet/find by chance | I came across an old diary |
| set up | establish | a clinic was set up in the village |

**Particles with a logic of their own:** *up* often completes (*finish, appear, build*), *off* suggests cancellation or departure, *out* suggests eruption or distribution, *down* suggests rejection or recording. When two options are grammatically possible, this direction sense breaks the tie.

**Preposition after 'different':** *different from* is the standard form in formal prose. **Preposition after 'compare'**: *compared to* (liken) vs *compared with* (examine differences) — in SSC usage both survive, but *compared to* is the safer default for similarity.

tricks.title: Governor chant
tricks.body: Underline the word governing the blank and recite its pair: depend—on, afraid—of, good—at, solution—to. Ten pairs cover most paper prepositions.

example.q: '...now pay residents a small sum to ___ the trees outside their homes.' Options: look after / look into / look down upon / look up to.
example.solution: Paying someone to care for trees → look after. *Look into* investigates, the other two are about respect/contempt.

tricks.title: Particle direction sense
tricks.body: Ask what the sentence does to the object: cancels it (*call off*), rejects it (*turn down*), erects it (*set up*). The particle encodes the action's direction.

tricks.title: Substitute the simple verb
tricks.body: Replace the phrasal option with a one-word verb in your head: look after = tend. The sentence must keep its meaning with the substitution; if not, that phrasal is wrong.

mistakes: Choosing a preposition by intuition from Hindi rather than by the English governor.
Splitting a phrasal verb: 'give way' needs its particle; 'gives way' without 'to' can also be the trap depending on the sentence.
Mixing *between* and *among* — two items take *between*, an indefinite group takes *among*.
Using *in* for years vs *on* for dates: 'in 2024' but 'on 15 August 2024'.
subtopics.notes:
### Preposition blanks: fixed pairs
English fixes a preposition to many verbs, adjectives and nouns, and logic rarely helps — the pair is a convention. The blank is usually the second half of such a pair, so your real task is to spot the first half and recall its partner.

### High-frequency fixed pairs
| First half | Correct pair | Wrong pair to avoid |
|---|---|---|
| ashamed | ashamed **of** | ashamed for |
| respond | respond **to** | respond on |
| apply (organisation) | apply **to** a bank | apply on |
| apply (post) | apply **for** a post | apply to a post |
| depend | depend **on** | depend from |
| prevent | prevent **from** + -ing | prevent to |
| insist | insist **on** + -ing | insist to |
| smell / taste | smell **of** garlic | smell with |
| arrive | arrive **at** a place, **in** a city | arrive to |
| married | married **to** | married with |
| according | according **to** records | according with |
| in spite | in spite **of** | in spite from |

### Prepositions of time: in, on, at
- **at** a clock or point: at 6 p.m., at noon, at night.
- **on** a day or date: on Sunday, on 15 August, on Sunday morning.
- **in** a longer period: in June, in 2019, in the morning, in winter.
- Duration with *since/for* with perfect tenses: since 2020 (point), for five years (length).

### Prepositions of place
- **at** a point on the map: at the bus stop, at the gate.
- **in** an enclosed space or area: in the room, in Erode, in India.
- **on** a surface or line: on the table, on the riverbank, on the wall.
- *away from*, *out of*, *into* show direction: cattle kept **away from** the edge.

### Phrasal verbs: the particle is the meaning
A phrasal verb = verb + particle, and the particle changes the meaning completely:
- **look after** = take care of; **look into** = investigate; **look down upon** = despise; **look up to** = admire.
- **put off** = postpone; **put down** = place / write; **put up with** = tolerate.
- **set up** = establish; **set out** = begin a journey; **set aside** = save or discard.
- **carry out** = perform; **carry on** = continue.
In the exam, translate the sentence's need into a meaning ("take care of the trees") and then find the phrasal verb with that meaning — never accept a phrasal verb just because it contains a familiar verb.

### Method for these blanks
1. Read the word before the blank (verb/adjective/noun) and the phrase after it.
2. If a fixed pair exists, the pair decides — no meaning test needed.
3. If it is a phrasal verb, state the needed meaning first, then match the particle.
4. For time/place, classify the noun: clock/point → at, day → on, period/enclosure → in.

### Quick revision
- Fixed pairs decide: ashamed of, respond to, depend on, married to, according to, in spite of.
- apply **to** an organisation, apply **for** a post.
- at a point, on a day, in a period or enclosure.
- Phrasal verb: decide the meaning first, then the particle (look after ≠ look into).
- Never translate prepositions from your mother tongue.

patterns.name: Preposition after a verb or adjective (fixed pair)
patterns.howToSpot: The blank follows a word like ashamed, respond, insist, smell and the options are single prepositions.
patterns.logic:
1. Identify the word before the blank.
2. Recall its fixed preposition (ashamed of, respond to, insist on).
3. Check the object after the blank — some words take different prepositions for different objects (apply TO a bank, apply FOR a post).

*Why it works:* the pair is a convention; once you spot the first half, only one option survives.

example.q: "The office responds (1) ______ every complaint within a day." (a) to (b) for (c) on (d) at
example.solution: The fixed pair is **respond to**: responds to every complaint. *Respond for/on/at* are not English.

patterns.name: Preposition of time or place
patterns.howToSpot: The blank sits before a clock time, a day, a period or a place, and the options are in/on/at/by/since/during type words.
patterns.logic:
1. Classify the noun after the blank: point of time → at; day or date → on; longer period → in; duration up to a limit → until/by; through a period → during.
2. For places: point → at, enclosure/area → in, surface/line → on.
3. Plug in the word and read the sentence as a full statement.

*Why it works:* the noun's kind forces the preposition; the other options break the classification.

example.q: "Suresh and his wife rarely watch television (1) ______ Sundays." (a) in (b) on (c) at (d) within
example.solution: Sundays = a day → **on**. *In* takes periods, *at* takes clock points, *within* takes a length of time.

patterns.name: Phrasal verb blank
patterns.howToSpot: The options are the same verb with different particles (put off/down/up) or different phrasal verbs with near meanings.
patterns.logic:
1. Say the needed meaning in plain words ('postpone small pleasures').
2. Match each option's meaning: put off = postpone, put down = place/write, put up with = tolerate.
3. Choose the phrasal verb whose meaning equals your plain-words version.

*Why it works:* the particle carries the meaning; translating the sentence first stops you from being hypnotised by the main verb.

example.q: "A man who cannot put (1) ______ small pleasures for a year does not deserve a big one." (a) off (b) down (c) up (d) in
example.solution: Needed meaning: postpone enjoying them → **put off**. *Put down* = place, *put up* = erect/tolerate (with 'with').

patterns.name: Preposition inside a fixed phrase
patterns.howToSpot: The blank is part of a set phrase: in spite of, according to, on behalf of, in charge of, with the help of.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the phrase after the blank (…of repeated warnings, …the committee's records).
2. Recall the complete phrase: in spite OF, according TO, on behalf OF.
3. Check that the completed phrase fits the sentence's logic (concession, source of information, representation).

*Why it works:* the phrase is one unit; half of it is given, so the other half is fixed.

example.q: "Contractors who delay the work are fined (1) ______ of repeated warnings." (a) due (b) in spite (c) instead (d) ahead
example.solution: **In spite of** repeated warnings = although they were warned many times. *Due of* is not English ('due to' has no 'of'), and 'fined instead of warnings' or 'ahead of warnings' makes no sense here — the sentence concedes the warnings and still fines.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The options are the same verb in different shapes (made/make/making) or tenses. Usually two or three of the five blanks in a passage are of this kind.
pyqPatterns.approach: Find the time anchor of the passage ('Last January', 'every morning', 'now') and keep only forms that stay inside that frame. Then check the subject: a singular subject needs the -s form in the present. A bare -ing form can never be the finite verb of a sentence.

example.q: 'Last January the terrace became a workshop. Every evening he and his son (1) ______ new kites.' Options: made/make/making/maker.
example.solution: Past anchor 'Last January' + habitual 'every evening' → simple past: made. 'Make' breaks the frame; 'making' is not finite.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The blank sits between two clauses, or at the start of a second sentence that comments on the first. Options are words like but, because, moreover, until.
pyqPatterns.approach: Compress each side of the blank into + or − (or cause/effect). Opposite directions → but/yet/although; a clause answering 'why' → because/since; a second supporting point after a semicolon → moreover; events on a clock → while/until/before. Then read the joined sentence aloud to confirm.

example.q: 'Business has not suffered at all; (1) ______, some customers now order a second cup.' Options: however/therefore/moreover/otherwise.
example.solution: Both clauses push the same way and the punctuation asks for a linking adverb → moreover.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The options are single prepositions (to/for/on) or particles (off/up/out) after a verb, adjective or fixed phrase.
pyqPatterns.approach: Most of these blanks are fixed pairs: ashamed of, respond to, depend on, apply to (organisation) / for (post), in spite of, according to. For phrasal verbs, say the needed meaning in plain words first ('postpone' → put off), then match the particle.

example.q: 'He is not ashamed (1) ______ his timetable.' Options: of/for/with/from.
example.solution: Fixed pair ashamed of → of. The other three do not exist with ashamed.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: All four options are grammatical in the blank; the sentence's meaning and the clue in a neighbouring clause must decide.
pyqPatterns.approach: Say the sentence's message in your own words, then keep the option that names exactly that idea. The clue is usually in the same sentence (often after a colon or semicolon); sometimes the next sentence confirms it. Cut options from the same broad field that do not match the precise idea.

example.q: 'The quiet here has a different (1) ______ from the quiet of their homes, where the television mutters.' Options: price/quality/length/colour.
example.solution: The next clause describes the character of the quiet → quality.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The blank completes a set phrase such as take advantage, make room, pay attention, keep a promise.
pyqPatterns.approach: Read the noun after the blank and recall its fixed partner verb. Do not translate from your mother tongue — the make/do/take swap is the classic trap. If two options seem possible, only the conventional partner is accepted in the exam.

example.q: 'The students (1) ______ full advantage of the extended hours.' Options: make/do/take/give.
example.solution: take (full) advantage of — 'do advantage' and 'make advantage' are not English.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The options differ only in number or person (is/are, gives/give), and the sentence has a long phrase between the subject and the verb, or an each/every/one-of structure.
pyqPatterns.approach: Cross out the words between the true subject and the verb, find the subject's number, then match the verb and the passage's time frame. 'The soil in his yard ___ too rocky' → soil is singular → is.

example.q: 'A group of volunteers ___ its own discipline.' Options: develop/develops/developing/had developed.
example.solution: True subject 'a group' is singular and the passage is in general present → develops.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The options are a, an, the (or their capital forms) before a noun.
pyqPatterns.approach: First mention or one of many → a/an (an before a vowel sound). Already known, already specified by a phrase, or one of a kind → the. General plural or uncountable idea often needs no article, so reject both when the noun is generic.

example.q: 'On festival day (1) ______ sky above the lane was full of kites.' Options: A/An/The/Some.
example.solution: 'The sky above the lane' is one specific sky → The.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Word whose answer needs the whole passage (theme / local-fit traps)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The options all fit the grammar and most fit the general topic; the correct one continues the passage's controlling idea, or the tempting one clashes with a line elsewhere.
pyqPatterns.approach: Read the full passage before answering and name its theme. Keep the option that stays inside the story's world and metaphor. Before finalising, re-read the passage with your answers — a locally fitting option that contradicts another line must go.

example.q: 'The market sells food, but what it really (1) ______ is company.' Options: paints/sells/measures/imports.
example.solution: The passage's metaphor is selling → sells. The other verbs break the metaphor that runs through the whole passage.

solvedExamples.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1).
solvedExamples.solution: The anchor 'Every morning' fixes habitual simple present, and the subject 'the city' is singular, so the verb takes -s: **awakens**. *Awaken* is the plural/base form, *awakened* is a finished past that clashes with the habitual present of the whole passage, and *awakening* cannot serve as the finite verb after 'the city fully'.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Time anchor first, agreement second: 'Every morning' + singular subject leaves exactly one form.
solvedExamples.passage: Every morning, before the city fully (1) ______, a quiet crowd gathers in the parks. Retired teachers, young joggers and mothers returning from the dairy booths share the same paths.

solvedExamples.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2).
solvedExamples.solution: Clause A is positive (the walk costs nothing, demands nothing); clause B is negative (very few continue it). Opposite directions demand a contrast connector: **yet**. *So* and *hence* announce a result and need both clauses pointing the same way; *because* would claim that the walk's cheapness is the *reason* few continue it — the opposite of the intended meaning.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Give the two clauses +/− signs: plus then minus = contrast connector (yet/but).
solvedExamples.passage: The morning walk costs nothing and demands no equipment, (2) ______ very few people manage to continue it beyond a fortnight.

solvedExamples.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (5).
solvedExamples.solution: The city pays residents a small sum so that they will *take care of* the trees outside their homes: **look after**. *Look into* means investigate (a complaint), *look down upon* means regard as inferior, and *look up to* means admire — none names the action that keeps trees alive. Substituting the simple verb *tend* confirms the choice.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Phrasal test: swap in the simple verb (tend). Only one option keeps the sentence's meaning.
solvedExamples.passage: Cities that have understood this simple point now pay residents a small sum to (5) ______ the trees outside their homes — and their streets are visibly greener.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1).
practice.solution: 'Every morning' sets habitual present and 'the city' is singular, so the finite verb takes -s: **awakens**. *Awakened* would break the habitual frame, *awaken* lacks agreement, and *awakening* is not a finite verb form.
practice.shortcut: Anchor + skeleton: 'every morning' + 'the city ___' → simple present with -s.
practice.passage: Every morning, before the city fully (1) ______, a quiet crowd gathers in the parks. Retired teachers, young joggers and mothers returning from the dairy booths share the same paths. The morning walk costs nothing and demands no equipment, (2) ______ very few people manage to continue it beyond a fortnight. Doctors point out that its benefits depend almost entirely on (3) ______; twenty minutes on Sunday cannot undo six days of sitting. Over the weeks, a regular walker begins to (4) ______ noticeable changes — lighter steps, deeper sleep and a steadier mood. Perhaps that is why a group that walks together (5) ______ its own quiet discipline: the ones who arrive late feel they have missed something worth keeping.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2).
practice.solution: The clauses move in opposite directions — the walk demands nothing (+), yet few sustain it (−). Contrast is required: **yet**. *So/hence* would wrongly make continuation scarce a *result* of the walk's simplicity; *because* reverses the logic entirely.
practice.shortcut: + clause, − clause → contrast word (yet/but).
practice.passage: Every morning, before the city fully (1) ______, a quiet crowd gathers in the parks. Retired teachers, young joggers and mothers returning from the dairy booths share the same paths. The morning walk costs nothing and demands no equipment, (2) ______ very few people manage to continue it beyond a fortnight. Doctors point out that its benefits depend almost entirely on (3) ______; twenty minutes on Sunday cannot undo six days of sitting. Over the weeks, a regular walker begins to (4) ______ noticeable changes — lighter steps, deeper sleep and a steadier mood. Perhaps that is why a group that walks together (5) ______ its own quiet discipline: the ones who arrive late feel they have missed something worth keeping.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (3).
practice.solution: The clause after the semicolon supplies the meaning: twenty minutes on Sunday cannot undo six days of sitting — benefits depend on doing it **regularly**. The noun naming that idea is *regularity*. *Equipment* contradicts the earlier line that the walk demands no equipment; luck and medicine are outside the sentence's logic.
practice.shortcut: Name the missing idea first ('consistency'), then match — the option echoing the next clause is the answer.
practice.passage: Every morning, before the city fully (1) ______, a quiet crowd gathers in the parks. Retired teachers, young joggers and mothers returning from the dairy booths share the same paths. The morning walk costs nothing and demands no equipment, (2) ______ very few people manage to continue it beyond a fortnight. Doctors point out that its benefits depend almost entirely on (3) ______; twenty minutes on Sunday cannot undo six days of sitting. Over the weeks, a regular walker begins to (4) ______ noticeable changes — lighter steps, deeper sleep and a steadier mood. Perhaps that is why a group that walks together (5) ______ its own quiet discipline: the ones who arrive late feel they have missed something worth keeping.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (4).
practice.solution: The list that follows — lighter steps, deeper sleep, steadier mood — names changes the walker actually feels: a regular walker begins to **experience** noticeable changes. *Abandon* and *postpone* contradict the praise, and *imagine* breaks the factual tone the passage maintains about doctors' findings.
practice.shortcut: Let the appositive list decide: the verb must introduce real, felt changes.
practice.passage: Every morning, before the city fully (1) ______, a quiet crowd gathers in the parks. Retired teachers, young joggers and mothers returning from the dairy booths share the same paths. The morning walk costs nothing and demands no equipment, (2) ______ very few people manage to continue it beyond a fortnight. Doctors point out that its benefits depend almost entirely on (3) ______; twenty minutes on Sunday cannot undo six days of sitting. Over the weeks, a regular walker begins to (4) ______ noticeable changes — lighter steps, deeper sleep and a steadier mood. Perhaps that is why a group that walks together (5) ______ its own quiet discipline: the ones who arrive late feel they have missed something worth keeping.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (5).
practice.solution: Strip the sentence to its skeleton: 'a group ___ its own quiet discipline'. The subject *a group* is singular and the passage speaks in general present, so: **develops**. *Develop* lacks agreement; *developing* cannot serve as the finite verb; *had developed* drags in a past perfect that has no anchor in this habitual, timeless statement.
practice.shortcut: Skeleton test: 'a group ___' → singular present, -s form.
practice.passage: Every morning, before the city fully (1) ______, a quiet crowd gathers in the parks. Retired teachers, young joggers and mothers returning from the dairy booths share the same paths. The morning walk costs nothing and demands no equipment, (2) ______ very few people manage to continue it beyond a fortnight. practice.solution: The sentence is a contrast: 'once half ___ … is now full by eight o'clock.' The word standing against *full* is **empty**. *Painted*, *carpeted* and *furnished* are real hall improvements, but none is the opposite of full — the contrast signal (once…now) decides.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1).
practice.solution: 'What began as a pastime has become a small ___: forty children … attend her free class.' A regular, established activity with forty regulars is a small **institution**. *Accident*, *complaint* and *excuse* carry negative or unrelated meanings that clash with the proud, growth story of the passage.
practice.shortcut: The colon lists the evidence (forty regulars) — the blank must name an established, grown activity.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2).
practice.solution: 'Chess does not ___ talent alone; it rewards habit.' The verb must mean 'need/demand': **require**. The sentence then balances talent against habit. *Refuse*, *print* and *pardon* are verbs, but 'chess refuses talent' or 'chess prints talent' says nothing the second clause can support.
practice.shortcut: The clause after the semicolon ('it rewards habit') tells you the verb means 'need'.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1).
practice.solution: Two actions happen at the same time: they read **while** the tea cools. *Until* would need the reading to stop when the tea cools, *unless* adds a condition, and *before* puts the reading earlier — none matches the picture of reading and cooling happening together.
practice.shortcut: Two overlapping actions → while.

The owner, Joseph, keeps a shelf of old magazines beside the stove, and customers read them (1) ______ their tea cools. His regulars first laughed at the shelf, (2) ______ today even senior nurses borrow his weeklies. Business has not suffered at all; (3) ______, some customers now order a second cup to finish an article. Nurses say they keep borrowing (4) ______ the magazines remind them of the hospital's own reading room.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2).
practice.solution: First they laughed at the shelf (−), now even nurses borrow from it (+): the two clauses point in opposite directions → contrast: **but**. *So* would make the laughing the cause of the borrowing, *because* reverses the logic, and *and* hides the turn the writer clearly makes.
practice.shortcut: Mark each clause + or −; opposite signs → but/yet.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (3).
practice.solution: 'Business has not suffered at all; (3) ___, some customers now order a second cup.' Both clauses push the same way (good, then even better), and the semicolon + comma asks for a linking adverb of addition: **moreover**. *However* turns the direction, *therefore* claims a result, *otherwise* adds a condition.
practice.shortcut: Same direction + semicolon-comma → moreover / furthermore.

practice.solution: Sales doubled (+ growth) ___ charging is a headache (− problem): the second clause turns against the first → **but**. *So* would wrongly make charging trouble a *result* of rising sales being good news, and *because* reverses cause and effect.
practice.shortcut: Good news vs bad news in one sentence → contrast.

Makers are aware of the problem; (3) ______, they have begun bundling a portable charger with every new scooter. Buyers should still check their building's wiring first, (4) ______ old lines sometimes cannot carry the load of an overnight charge.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2).
practice.solution: The scooter is left at night and stays there up to a time limit: 'may stay there **until** morning'. *Since* needs a starting point ('since nine o'clock'), *after* would put its stay after the morning, and *by* fits a deadline ('finish by morning'), not a continuing state.
practice.shortcut: A state continuing up to a point → until.

practice.solution: 'Makers are aware of the problem; (3) ___, they have begun bundling a portable charger.' practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (1).
practice.solution: The exchange scheme is the *cause* of the change: because every plastic bag was swapped for a cloth one, visitors stopped bringing plastic at all. The ban has even spread beyond the temple; (3) ______, the village panchayat passed a similar rule for its weekly market.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (2).
practice.solution: '___ the ban, monkeys used to scatter torn plastic along the paths; the slopes are clean now.' The monkeys' habit belongs to the time **before** the ban — the second half states the present. *After* reverses the order, and the logic connectors cannot place events on a clock.

practice.shortcut: away → from. Read the whole phrase around the blank.
practice.passage: The lake behind the sugar mill had become a grey pond that smelled (1) ______ chemicals. Three years ago the villagers formed a committee and decided to set (2) ______ a small fund for desilting the lake bed. Fish returned the following spring. The committee now guards the lake strictly: anyone caught dumping waste must pay a fine, and cattle are kept away (3) ______ the shallow edge by a low stone fence. (4) ______ the committee's records, the lake has not gone dry even once since the desilting.

practice.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number (4).
practice.solution: The sentence cites a source of information: '___ the committee's records, the lake has not gone dry…' The phrase for quoting a source is **according to**. *Owing to* means because of (and would make the records the cause of the lake's health), *in spite of* contradicts the logic, *along the records* is not a phrase.
practice.shortcut: Blank + 'the records' + a reported fact → According to.
